defs: Certificate
A digitally signed document that binds an identity or system to a public key.

course.learn: A Certificate Authority (CA) is a trusted entity that signs digital certificates and vouches that a public key is associated with the named identity. Root CAs anchor trust; intermediate CAs help issue certificates without exposing the root key constantly.
course.why: Certificates are only useful if clients can trust the entity that signed them.
course.example: A browser trusts a site certificate because an intermediate CA signed it and that intermediate chains to a trusted root CA.
course.exam: Root CA = trust anchor. Intermediate CA = delegated issuer. Private/internal CAs serve an organization; public CAs issue publicly trusted certificates.

course.learn: Digital certificates can be issued for different purposes and scopes, such as a single host, multiple names, wildcard subdomains, code signing, users, email, or devices.
course.why: The certificate must match how the identity and key will actually be used.
course.example: A wildcard certificate for *.example.com can cover many first-level subdomains, while a single-name certificate covers one specific host name.
course.exam: CompTIA may ask which certificate type best fits one host, many SAN names, wildcard subdomains, or signing code.

defs: Certificate
A digitally signed document that binds an identity or system to a public key.

course.learn: A Certificate Signing Request (CSR) contains identity information and a public key that an applicant sends to a CA when requesting a certificate. The private key should remain with the applicant.
course.why: The CA needs the public key and verified identity information in order to issue a certificate without receiving the private key.
course.example: A web server generates a key pair locally, sends a CSR containing the public key to a CA, and receives a signed certificate.
course.exam: Private key stays private. CSR carries the public key and certificate-request information.

slides.teach: Read the source points, then explain the slide without looking. On Security+, recognition is not enough—you should be able to apply the concept to a scenario.

course.learn: A root of trust is a highly trusted foundation—often hardware, firmware, or a protected key—from which later integrity and identity decisions are derived.
course.why: If the foundation is trustworthy, systems can build a chain of verification upward through boot firmware, operating systems, and applications.
course.example: Secure Boot verifies each boot component before allowing the next component to execute, starting from a hardware-backed trust anchor.
course.exam: Root of trust and chain of trust appear in secure boot, TPM, HSM, certificate, and device-integrity scenarios.

breakdown.term: Requires the hardware to be trusted before software
breakdown.explanation: Hardware security risk includes vulnerable firmware, malicious peripherals, insecure interfaces, unsupported devices, and physical tampering.

breakdown.term: Is based on the security chain
breakdown.explanation: This contributes to reducing risk in the broader Certificates design and should be evaluated as part of defense in depth.

breakdown.term: Support secure boot, secure enclave, and anti-tamper
breakdown.explanation: A secure enclave is an isolated execution area designed to protect sensitive computations and secrets even if the main operating system is compromised.
Within Root of Trust, this is a specific factor you should be able to recognize and explain. Connect it to the purpose of Certificates rather than memorizing the phrase by itself.

course.check_q: Without looking back, explain Root of Trust and describe at least two key ideas from this section.
course.check_a: A root of trust is a highly trusted foundation—often hardware, firmware, or a protected key—from which later integrity and identity decisions are derived. Key ideas include: Requires the hardware to be trusted before software; Is based on the security chain; Support secure boot, secure enclave, and anti-tamper; resistance.
points: Requires the hardware to be trusted before software
Is based on the security chain
Support secure boot, secure enclave, and anti-tamper
